documents.text:
197 FERC ¶ 61,091
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
	
Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER AUTHORIZING DISPOSITION OF JURISDICTIONAL FACILITIES

(Issued November 4, 2026)

On May 8, 2026, as amended September 1, 2026, pursuant to section 203(a)(1) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) and Part 33 of the Commission’s regulations, Long Ridge Energy Generation LLC (Long Ridge Energy Generation) and Long Ridge Retail Electric Supplier LLC (Long Ridge Retail, together with Long Ridge Energy Generation, Applicants) filed an application (Application) requesting approval for a proposed transaction whereby MARA USA Corporation (MARA Buyer) will indirectly acquire 100% of the membership interests in Applicants from Ohio River Partners Holdco LLC (Ohio River Holdco) and Ohio River Partners Finance LLC (Ohio River Finance) (Proposed Transaction).   
We have reviewed the Proposed Transaction under the Commission’s Merger Policy Statement.  As discussed below, we authorize the Proposed Transaction as consistent with the public interest.
Background
Description of Applicants and Affiliates
Applicants state that Long Ridge Energy Generation owns and operates the Long Ridge Energy Generation Project, an approximately 522 megawatt (MW) combined cycle, natural gas-fired electric generation facility in Ohio, within the Long Ridge Energy Terminal (Long Ridge Facility).  Applicants note that the Long Ridge Facility is part of an existing industrial property that was the site of the former Ormet Primary Aluminum Corporation aluminum reduction facility.  Applicants state that the Long Ridge Facility is “…interconnected with transmission facilities owned and controlled by AEP Ohio, within the [PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM)] regional transmission organization’s AEP-RTO submarket.”  Applicants further state that Long Ridge Energy Generation is an exempt wholesale generator (EWG) under the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 2005 (PUHCA 2005) and is authorized by the Commission to sell energy, capacity, and ancillary services at market-based rates.  Applicants represent that Long Ridge Energy Generation does not own or control any other electric transmission facilities other than the limited interconnection facilities needed to connect the Long Ridge Facility with the PJM transmission system.
Applicants state that Long Ridge Energy Generation owns an approximately    two-mile intrastate natural gas service line that is operated by Eureka Midstream and is dedicated exclusively to serving the Long Ridge Facility.  They explain that natural gas volumes produced by Ohio Gasco LLC, a natural gas drilling and production company, which is owned by Long Ridge Energy Generation’s immediate parent, Long Ridge Energy LLC, are transported through the service line to the Long Ridge Facility via an interconnection to the Eureka Midstream intrastate pipeline.  
Applicants state that Long Ridge Retail is authorized to sell energy, capacity, and ancillary services at market-based rates within the PJM market only, and does not own or control any generating facilities or assets or any transmission facilities.  Additionally, Applicants state that Long Ridge Retail also does not purchase any energy and/or capacity from an unaffiliated third party pursuant to a long-term firm agreement.
Applicants state that they are wholly owned subsidiaries of Long Ridge Energy & Power LLC, which is 99% owned by Ohio River Holdco and 1% by Ohio River Finance, which is, in turn, 100% owned by Ohio River Holdco.  Applicants further state that Ohio River Holdco is a directly wholly owned subsidiary of FTAI Infrastructure Inc. (FTAI Infrastructure).  Applicants represent that FTAI Infrastructure is a publicly traded company and that the only entities that own, hold, or control with power to vote 10% or more of the voting equity in FTAI Infrastructure are GCM Grosvenor and the Washington State Investment Board.  They state that the remaining voting equity interests in FTAI Infrastructure are held by other public shareholders.  Ohio River Holdco and Ohio River Finance are together referred to as the FTAI Infrastructure Sellers. 
Description of MARA Buyer and Affiliates
Applicants state that MARA Buyer is a wholly owned subsidiary of MARA Holdings, Inc. (MARA), which is a digital infrastructure company that is principally engaged in producing or “mining” digital assets.  Applicants represent that the only shareholders that hold 10% or more of MARA are BlackRock, Inc. (BlackRock) and The Vanguard Group (Vanguard).  Applicants contend that while BlackRock and Vanguard would each be deemed an ultimate upstream affiliate of MARA, and of Applicants, after consummation of the Proposed Transaction, they do not hold seats on MARA’s board of directors and do not otherwise exert any control over MARA.  Therefore, Applicants state that none of BlackRock’s or Vanguard’s other holdings can be deemed to be affiliated with MARA.
Applicants state that, in connection with MARA’s principal digital asset mining activities, MARA engages in owning and operating cryptocurrency mining facilities, or data centers, and activates a portion of its cryptocurrency holdings through lending, structured trading and collateralized financing arrangements.
Applicants state that Great Plains Windpark Legacy, LLC (Great Plains Windpark) owns and operates the Great Plains Wind Farm (Great Plains Facility), an approximately 114 MW wind energy facility in Texas, which is interconnected with the transmission system owned by Southwestern Public Service Company, within the Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) market.  They state that Great Plains is an EWG and is authorized by the Commission to sell energy, capacity, and ancillary services at market-based rates, and that all of the output of the Great Plains Facility is uncommitted and sold in the wholesale markets operated by SPP.  According to Applicants, with the exception of Great Plains Windpark, neither MARA Buyer nor MARA owns or controls, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the voting equity interests in (or own or control any voting equity interests together with the right to appoint any officer or director with respect to) any public utilities, electric generation facilities, electric transmission facilities, any public utility with a franchised service territory in the United States, or inputs to electric power production in the United States.  
Description of the Proposed Transaction
Applicants state that the terms of the Proposed Transaction are set forth in the Equity Purchase Agreement dated April 29, 2026, by and among FTAI Infrastructure Sellers, MARA Buyer, and, solely for the purposes specified therein, FTAI Infrastructure and MARA.  Applicants also state that, pursuant to the Equity Purchase Agreement, MARA Buyer will indirectly acquire 100% of the membership interests in Applicants from FTAI Infrastructure Sellers.
Notice of Filing and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of the Application was published in the Federal Register, with interventions and protests due on or before May 29, 2026.  
Timely motions to intervene were filed by Public Citizen, Inc. and Monitoring Analytics, LLC, acting in its capacity as the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (PJM IMM).
On May 29, 2026, the PJM IMM filed comments (PJM IMM Comments).
On June 1, 2026, PJM and American Electric Power Service Corporation (AEP) each filed motions to intervene out-of-time.
On June 8, 2026, Applicants filed an answer to the PJM IMM Comments (Applicants Answer).
On August 25, 2026, a deficiency letter was issued (Deficiency Letter).  On September 1, 2026, Applicants filed a response to the Deficiency Letter (Deficiency Letter Response).
Notice of the Deficiency Letter Response was published in the Federal Register, with interventions and protests due on or before September 15, 2026.
On September 15, 2026, the PJM IMM filed comments on the Deficiency Letter Response (PJM IMM Deficiency Response Comments).
On September 23, 2026, Applicants filed an answer to the PJM IMM Deficiency Response Comments (Applicants Second Answer).
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,              18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the timely, unopposed motions to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding.

Pursuant to Rule 214(d) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,         18 C.F.R. § 385.214(d), we grant PJM’s and AEP’s late-filed motions to intervene given their interest in the proceeding, the early stage of the proceeding, and the absence of undue prejudice or delay.
Rule 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the Applicants’ answers because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters
FPA Section 203 Standard of Review
FPA section 203(a)(4) requires the Commission to approve proposed dispositions, consolidations, acquisitions, or changes in control if the Commission determines that the proposed transaction will be consistent with the public interest.  The Commission’s analysis of whether a proposed transaction is consistent with the public interest generally involves consideration of three factors:  (1) the effect on competition; (2) the effect on rates; and (3) the effect on regulation.  FPA section 203(a)(4) also requires the Commission to find that the proposed transaction “will not result in cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or the pledge or encumbrance of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company, unless the Commission determines that the cross-subsidization, pledge, or encumbrance will be consistent with the public interest.”  The Commission’s regulations establish verification and informational requirements for entities that seek a determination that a proposed transaction will not result in inappropriate cross-subsidization or pledge or encumbrance of utility assets.
Analysis of the Proposed Transaction
Effect on Horizonal Competition
Applicants’ Analysis
Applicants claim that the Proposed Transaction will have no adverse effect on competition as it presents no horizontal market power concerns.  They state that FPA section 203 applicants are not required to submit a horizontal market power analysis performed in accordance with the Commission’s Merger Policy Statement where the combining “entities do not currently conduct business in the same geographic markets or …the extent of the business transactions in the same geographic markets is de minimis.”  Applicants state that the relevant market is the PJM market, where the Long Ridge Facility is located, and because none of MARA Buyer or its affiliates owns or controls any generation capacity that is located in the PJM market or any PJM submarket, there is no overlap.  Applicants conclude that no horizontal market power analysis is required.
PJM IMM Comments
The PJM IMM states that, on November 5, 2024, MARA Buyer acquired two operational data centers located in Ohio, with one physically located at the same site as the Long Ridge Facility.  The PJM IMM argues that the Application does not clarify how the capacity from the Long Ridge Facility will be treated in the future and how MARA Buyer intends to use the capacity to serve data center load while leaving the capacity and energy in the PJM markets.  The PJM IMM asserts that removing the capacity from the market would be a form of withholding and make the PJM markets less competitive and increase costs for other customers.  The PJM IMM states that the Proposed Transaction should only be approved with the condition that the full generation capacity of the Long Ridge Facility stays in the PJM markets.
The PJM IMM asserts that PJM’s capacity market is extremely tight and that it was actually short in the 2026/2027 and 2027/2028 base residual auctions.  The PJM IMM represents that the capacity market is likely to remain extremely tight for the foreseeable future, resulting in prices that are extremely high by historical standards, which increases the potential impact of market power.  The PJM IMM maintains that capacity owners in PJM were pivotal in almost all reliability pricing model auctions prior to the current extreme conditions in the capacity market and that the current market shortage conditions due to growing data center load amplify that market power by making every individual capacity resource pivotal.  The PJM IMM contends that it is consistent with the public interest to condition the approval of transactions that increase market power on behavioral commitments that address market power.  Here, the PJM IMM argues that MARA must commit to not remove the capacity of the Long Ridge Facility from the PJM market to serve data center load.
The PJM IMM further maintains that the Proposed Transaction threatens the reliability and competitiveness of the PJM markets, and therefore is not consistent with the public interest, if it results in the removal of existing capacity and energy from the markets to serve large data center loads.  It argues that the impact on competition from load growth from data centers is the most critical issue affecting PJM markets and the public interest in competitive outcomes today and that a comprehensive solution has not been defined.  The PJM IMM contends that conditioning authority under FPA section 203 can and should be invoked today to address a new issue requiring priority attention, and that the condition recommended, to not remove resources from the markets to serve data center load, is less burdensome than the requirement to provide open access was in the mid-1990s.
According to the PJM IMM, removing all or part of an existing capacity from the capacity market by MARA is a potential exercise of market power in the form of physical withholding, which would have a negative impact on the competitiveness of PJM markets and on the rates paid by the customers in PJM markets.  The PJM IMM states that the Long Ridge Facility represents 522 MW of capacity, which is a material quantity in an already deficient market.  The PJM IMM represents that withdrawal of this capacity would worsen the supply shortfall that caused PJM to clear short in the 2026/2027 and 2027/2028 base residual auctions, driving capacity prices higher for all PJM customers.  
The PJM IMM argues that the Proposed Transaction, without a condition that the Long Ridge Facility capacity fully remain in the PJM market, would result in MARA having an increased incentive and ability to exercise market power.  The PJM IMM represents that the removal of an economic resource from the market constitutes physical withholding and is a mechanism to exercise market power.  The PJM IMM further argues that neither the Commission’s merger policy orders nor the PJM Tariff explicitly addresses the removal of capacity resources to serve data centers, and that the Commission’s review under FPA section 203 is the proper venue to evaluate whether new ownership would result in the ability and incentive to exercise market power, and whether the proposed transaction would be consistent with the public interest.
Applicants Answer
Applicants argue that the PJM IMM’s comments are unfounded and beyond the scope of this proceeding.  Applicants again claim that the Proposed Transaction satisfies the requirements of FPA section 203 and reiterate statements in the Application.  Applicants argue that the PJM IMM’s comments do not rebut the showings that the Proposed Transaction will have no adverse effects on competition, rates, or regulation, and will not result in cross-subsidization.  Applicants assert that, instead, the PJM IMM’s comments are unrelated to the FPA section 203 standard of review.
Applicants argue further that the PJM IMM provides no authority to support the claim that serving large load customers constitutes an inappropriate exercise of market power, and that the Application does not propose the removal of generation capacity from the PJM market.  According to Applicants, the PJM IMM offers nothing more than the explanation that serving increasing load with existing supply increases supply prices, which is restating the principles of supply and demand, not a demonstration of “withholding.”  Applicants argue that a bilateral sale of generation from a generator in a market to a load in a market cannot conceivably amount to any sort of withholding.  Applicants assert that adopting that position would place many generators in every Commission-jurisdictional wholesale market that sell power bilaterally in a position where they have unwittingly engaged in manipulative behavior by selling to a “disfavored” load.  Applicants assert that to the extent the PJM IMM wishes to raise these industry-wide policy issues to ensure that the Commission’s rules for service to data center load are consistent with the policy objectives of various federal and state leaders, any such concerns are better addressed in other proceedings through other more suitable mechanisms.
Deficiency Letter and Response
The Deficiency Letter requested that Applicants confirm whether the acquisitions of voting shares of MARA, by both BlackRock and Vanguard, conform to the fact pattern contemplated in each of those investment companies’ respective blanket authorizations under section 203(a)(2) such that NextEra could apply for purposes of determining BlackRock’s and Vanguard’s affiliations with MARA.  In the Deficiency Letter Response, Applicants state that BlackRock’s and Vanguard’s acquisition of voting shares in MARA conform to the fact pattern of BlackRock’s and Vanguard’s respective blanket authorizations such that NextEra applies to their shares in MARA.  Applicants maintain that BlackRock and Vanguard each hold non-controlling interests of more than 10% and below 20% in MARA, consistent with the terms of their respective blanket authorizations.  Applicants further represent that BlackRock and Vanguard have each filed Schedule 13Gs with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) with respect to their shares in MARA, a U.S. Traded Utility “as defined in the context of such blanket authorizations,” and also included MARA in their respective quarterly reports to the Commission which disclose holdings of voting securities greater that 1% in U.S. Traded Utilities.  Applicants also assert that neither BlackRock nor Vanguard has attempted to exercise control over the day-to-day management or operations of MARA and, by virtue of their respective blanket authorizations and their respective Schedule 13G filings, both have committed to not exercising control over MARA.
The Deficiency Letter also requested that Applicants confirm whether MARA is an investment management subsidiary of either BlackRock or Vanguard and requested additional information about MARA Buyer’s business activities.  Applicants responded that MARA is not an investment management subsidiary of either BlackRock or Vanguard, and that BlackRock and Vanguard are non-controlling shareholders in MARA.  Applicants also explained that MARA Buyer is a U.S. operating and investment subsidiary of MARA and that MARA acquires, develops, owns, and operates large-scale data center and related energy infrastructure in the United States through MARA Buyer and its subsidiaries.
The Deficiency Letter further requested that Applicants provide a horizontal competitive analysis screen that treats BlackRock and Vanguard as affiliates of MARA, or explain why such a horizontal competitive analysis screen is not required.  Applicants responded that a horizontal competitive analysis is not required under NextEra because each of BlackRock and Vanguard remains subject to the conditions of their blanket authorizations and have filed Schedule 13Gs and quarterly reports to the Commission with respect to MARA, and expressly committed to not exercise control.
PJM IMM Deficiency Response Comments
The PJM IMM argues that the Deficiency Letter Response does not provide sufficient information to assure that the blanket authorization requirements are met because it is not clear that BlackRock and Vanguard do not have influence over the day-to-day management and operations of MARA.  The PJM IMM maintains that BlackRock is affiliated with 4.5 gigawatts (GW) of capacity in PJM through blanket authorizations and another 2.3 GW of capacity in PJM through controlling ownership positions.  The PJM IMM contends that this high level of affiliation requires a high level of scrutiny and that, as the largest shareholder of MARA, BlackRock has incentives to influence MARA’s operational decisions to benefit its own data center development and/or its generation units.  The PJM IMM also argues that while Applicants assert that filing a Schedule 13G with the SEC is conclusive evidence that an investor lacks control, there are many instances where Schedule 13G can be misused or lacks sufficient information to determine control and that more evidence is required to demonstrate that BlackRock and Vanguard have not exercised, and will not exercise, control over the day-to-day management of MARA.  The PJM IMM argues that:  (1) Applicants should be required to disclose all communication with Vanguard and BlackRock and (2) Vanguard and BlackRock should be required to adhere to publicly stated proxy voting rules that prevent any attempt to influence company decisions or policies.  Further, the PJM IMM requests that the Commission either reject the Application or continue to find the Application deficient until Applicants demonstrate that all blanket authorization requirements are met.
Applicants Second Answer
Applicants respond to the PJM IMM Deficiency Response Comments, asserting that the comments are beyond the scope of the Commission’s evaluation of the Proposed Transaction.  They contend that the PJM IMM wrongly suggests that Applicants rely exclusively on the submission of Schedule 13G filings by BlackRock and Vanguard to demonstrate that both entities lack control over MARA.  Applicants maintain that the Deficiency Letter Response confirms that BlackRock’s and Vanguard’s shares in MARA are held pursuant to their respective blanket authorizations, which require both BlackRock and Vanguard to adhere to numerous conditions to prevent the ability to control utilities.  Applicants assert that the Commission has held that so long as such institutional investors comply with the conditions imposed by their specific section 203 blanket authorizations, there is no common control to make those utilities affiliates.Applicants also argue that the PJM IMM’s request for more evidence that BlackRock and Vanguard have not and will not exercise control over the day-to-day management of MARA is outside the scope of this proceeding and that if the Commission determines that modifications to the conditions of the blanket authorization orders are required, it must do so in another proceeding.  Finally, Applicants maintain that a horizontal competitive analysis screen is unnecessary because NextEra applies and requiring this analysis would directly conflict with Commission precedent.
Commission Determination
In analyzing whether a proposed transaction will adversely affect horizontal competition, the Commission examines the effects on concentration in the generation markets and whether the proposed transaction otherwise creates the incentive and ability to engage in behavior harmful to competition, such as withholding of generation.  
Based on Applicants’ representations, we find that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on horizontal competition in the PJM market.  Under        section 33.3(a)(2) of the Commission’s regulations, applicants seeking authorization under FPA section 203 are not required to submit a horizontal market power analysis where the combining “entities do not currently conduct business in the same geographic markets or . . . the extent of the business transactions in the same geographic markets is de minimis” and “no intervenor has alleged that one of the merging entities is a perceived potential competitor in the same geographic market as the other.”  Based on Applicants’ representations and the facts of this case, we find that MARA Buyer is not affiliated with 
any generation capacity in PJM and thus there is no overlap in the same geographic market.  Accordingly, consistent with Commission precedent, Applicants need not provide any further analysis.
We are not persuaded by the PJM IMM’s argument that the Commission should   require MARA to not remove the capacity of the Long Ridge Facility from the PJM market to serve data center load.  The PJM IMM argues that removal of the Long Ridge Facility to serve data center load would constitute physical withholding which would negatively impact the competitiveness of the capacity markets on the rates paid by the customers in PJM and impact reliability.  The Commission’s evaluation of a proposed transaction’s effect on competition, and in particular, economic withholding, considers whether the proposed transaction otherwise creates the incentive and ability to engage in behavior harmful to competition, such as withholding of generation.  MARA Buyer does not have generation in PJM that would provide it with an incentive to physically withhold generation capacity or forego sales from the Long Ridge Facility to increase prices in the capacity market to benefit itself.  Thus, based on the facts of this case, the Proposed Transaction does not result in an incentive for MARA Buyer to withhold the Long Ridge Facility as the Commission evaluates that issue under its FPA section 203 policy.
For similar reasons, we reject the PJM IMM’s request that the Commission condition approval of the Proposed Transaction on Applicants committing not to remove in the Long Ridge Facility from the PJM market to serve data center load.  We note that the removal of any of Applicants’ generation facilities from the PJM market is governed by the PJM Tariff, including any revisions and changes to the PJM Tariff directed by the Commission in Docket No. EL25-49-000, where, among other things, the Commission addressed the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to Interconnection Customers serving Co-Located Load, or in response to the Commission’s order in Docket No. EL26-67.  For these reasons, we conclude that any additional specific commitment requirements are not necessary here.
Further, we find that a horizontal market power analysis that accounts for BlackRock’s and Vanguard’s and their affiliates’ holdings is not required.  MARA is now a U.S. Traded Utility and Applicants have represented that BlackRock and Vanguard have treated MARA as being held under their respective section 203(a)(2) blanket authorizations and reported MARA in their 2026 quarterly reports submitted to the Commission.  Therefore, consistent with NextEra, which found that “the institutional investors subject to a section 203(a)(2) blanket authorization order lack the ability to control the utilities whose voting securities they acquire,” we find that Applicants have shown that BlackRock and Vanguard lack the ability to control MARA and thus no horizontal market power analysis is required.
Finally, with respect to the PJM IMM’s concerns regarding BlackRock and Vanguard’s influence over MARA, we are not persuaded by the PJM IMM’s argument that the Commission should reject the Proposed Transaction.  Because we have found that BlackRock and Vanguard hold MARA’s voting securities consistent with the conditions of their section 203(a)(2) blanket authorization orders, we find that, consistent with NextEra, BlackRock and Vanguard lack the ability to control MARA.  Further, there is no evidence in the record that either BlackRock or Vanguard has used its holdings for purposes of influence or to exert market power.  Therefore, we reject the PJM IMM’s request to impose additional conditions on Applicants as the Proposed Transaction will have no adverse effect on competition.
Effect on Vertical Competition
Applicants’ Analysis
Applicants contend that the Proposed Transaction will have no adverse effect on vertical competition because it does not raise any vertical market power concerns.  According to Applicants, the Proposed Transaction does not involve any electric transmission facilities, other than interests in limited facilities used to interconnect the Long Ridge Facility to the transmission grid.  Applicants state further that the Commission has routinely accepted that ownership of assets such as the approximately two-mile intrastate natural gas service line operated by Eureka Midstream does not create vertical market power.  Additionally, Applicants represent that MARA Buyer does not own or control any electric transmission facilities in the PJM market, and that MARA Buyer does not own or control any upstream inputs to electricity products in the PJM market.  Applicants state that neither MARA nor its affiliates, including MARA Buyer, have erected barriers to entry in any U.S. electricity market.  Applicants assert that the Proposed Transaction presents no vertical market power concerns and that no vertical market power analysis is required.
Commission Determination
In analyzing whether a proposed transaction presents vertical market power concerns, the Commission considers the vertical combination of upstream inputs, such as natural gas transmission or natural gas supply or fuel, with downstream generating capacity and transmission.  As the Commission has previously found, transactions that combine electric generation assets with inputs to generating power can harm competition if the transaction increases an entity’s ability or incentive to exercise vertical market power in wholesale electricity markets.  For example, by denying rival entities access to inputs or by raising their input costs, an entity created by a transaction could impede entry of new competitors or inhibit existing competitors’ ability to undercut an attempted price increase in the downstream wholesale electricity market.
Based on Applicants’ representations, we find that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on vertical competition because the Proposed Transaction does not involve any electric transmission facilities, other than interests in limited facilities used to interconnect the Long Ridge Facility to the transmission grid.  With respect to Long Ridge Energy Generation’s approximately two-mile intrastate natural gas service line operated by Eureka Midstream and dedicated exclusively to serving the Long Ridge Facility, we note that the Commission has adopted a rebuttable presumption that ownership or control of such inputs does not allow an entity to erect barriers to entry.  In addition, MARA Buyer does not own or control any electric transmission facilities or any upstream inputs to electricity products in the PJM market.  Furthermore, the Proposed Transaction will not result in a combination of generation facilities with transmission facilities or other upstream relevant products in the relevant market, and, accordingly, a vertical market power analysis is not required.  Therefore, we find that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on vertical competition.
Effect on Rates
Applicants’ Analysis
Applicants assert that the Proposed Transaction will not adversely affect rates because all sales of electric energy, capacity and ancillary services by Applicants will continue to be made at market-based rates after the consummation of the Proposed Transaction.  They further state that none of Applicants, MARA Buyer, or any of MARA Buyer’s affiliates has any electric transmission customers or captive wholesale customers whose rates could be affected by the Proposed Transaction.
Commission Determination
Based on Applicants’ representations, we find that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on rates.  With respect to wholesale power rates, the Commission has previously stated that, when there are market-based rates, the effect on wholesale rates is not of concern “because market-based rates will not be affected by the seller’s cost of service and, thus, will not be adversely affected by the [proposed transaction].”  Here, Applicants represent that all wholesale sales of electric energy, capacity, and certain ancillary services will continue to be made pursuant to their market-based rate tariffs and related agreements.  With respect to transmission customers, we note that none of Applicants, MARA Buyer, or any of MARA Buyer’s affiliates has any electric transmission customers.  We therefore the Proposed Transaction will have no effect on transmission rates.  For these reasons, we find that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on rates.
Effect on Regulation
Applicants’ Analysis
Applicants claim that the Proposed Transaction will not have an adverse effect on the effectiveness of federal or state regulation because, following the consummation of the Proposed Transaction, Applicants will remain subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction to the same extent it is today.  Additionally, Applicants state that the Proposed Transaction will have no impact on the effectiveness of state regulation because neither Applicants nor MARA Buyer are subject to state rate regulation.
Commission Determination
The Commission’s review of a transaction’s effect on regulation focuses on ensuring that it does not result in a regulatory gap.  As to whether a proposed transaction will have an effect on state regulation, the Commission explained in the Merger Policy Statement that it ordinarily will not set the issue of the effect of a proposed transaction on state regulatory authority for a trial-type hearing where a state has authority to act on the proposed transaction.  However, if the state lacks this authority and raises concerns about the effect on regulation, the Commission may set the issue for hearing and it will address such circumstances on a case-by-case basis.  
Based on Applicants’ representations, we find no evidence that either state or federal regulation will be impaired by the Proposed Transaction.  There is no evidence that the Proposed Transaction will create a regulatory gap.  Applicants represent that the Proposed Transaction will not affect federal regulation because Applicants will remain subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction to the same extent after the consummation of the Proposed Transaction.  Additionally, Applicants state that the Proposed Transaction will not have an impact on state regulation because neither Applicants nor MARA Buyer are subject to state regulation.  Finally, we note that no party alleges that regulation, state or federal, would be impaired by the Proposed Transaction, and no state commission has requested that the Commission address the issue of the effect on state regulation.
Cross-Subsidization
Applicants’ Analysis
Applicants state that the Proposed Transaction falls within the Commission’s “safe harbor” under FPA section 203(a)(4) for transactions that do not involve any franchised public utility with captive customers, such that a detailed explanation and evidentiary support to demonstrate a lack of cross-subsidization is not required.  Applicants state that they nevertheless provide, in Exhibit M, representations that, based on the facts and circumstances knows to Applicants or that are reasonably foreseeable, the Proposed Transaction will not result in, at the time of the Proposed Transaction or in the future, cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or the pledge or encumbrance of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company.
Commission Determination
Based on Applicants’ representations, we find that the Proposed Transaction will not result in the cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company by a utility company, or in a pledge or encumbrance of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company.  We note that no party has argued otherwise.
Other Considerations
Information and/or systems connected to the Bulk Power System involved in this transaction may be subject to reliability and cybersecurity standards approved by the Commission pursuant to FPA section 215.  Compliance with these standards is mandatory and enforceable regardless of the physical location of the affiliates or investors, information database, and operating systems.  If affiliates, personnel or investors are not authorized for access to such information and/or systems connected to the Bulk Power System, a public utility is obligated to take the appropriate measures to deny access to this information and/or the equipment/software connected to the Bulk Power System.  The mechanisms that deny access to information, procedures, software, equipment, etc., must comply with all applicable reliability and cybersecurity standards. The Commission, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, or the relevant regional entity may audit compliance with reliability and cybersecurity standards.
FPA section 301(c) gives the Commission authority to examine the books and records of any person who controls, directly or indirectly, a jurisdictional public utility insofar as the books and records relate to transactions with or the business of such public utility.  The approval of the Proposed Transaction is based on such examination ability.  In addition, applicants subject to PUHCA 2005 are subject to the record-keeping and books and records requirements of PUHCA 2005.
Section 35.42 of the Commission’s regulations requires that sellers with market-based rate authority timely report to the Commission any change in status that would reflect a departure from the characteristics the Commission relied upon in granting market-based rate authority.  To the extent that a transaction authorized under FPA section 203 results in a change in status, sellers that have market-based rates are advised that they must comply with the requirements of section 35.42.
The Commission orders:
The Proposed Transaction is hereby authorized, as discussed in the body of this order.
Applicants must inform the Commission of any material change in circumstances that departs from the facts or representations that the Commission relied upon in authorizing the Proposed Transaction within 30 days from the date of the material change in circumstances.
The foregoing authorization is without prejudice to the authority of the Commission or any other regulatory body with respect to rates, service, accounts, valuation, estimates or determinations of costs, or any other matter whatsoever now pending or which may come before the Commission.
Nothing in this order shall be construed to imply acquiescence in any estimate or determination of cost or any valuation of property claimed or asserted.
The Commission retains authority under sections 203(b) and 309 of the FPA to issue supplemental orders as appropriate.
Applicants shall make any appropriate filings under section 205 of the FPA, as necessary, to implement the Proposed Transaction.
Applicants shall notify the Commission within 10 days of the date on which the Proposed Transaction is consummated.
